newsitem.title: USA: Clinton announces PBGC surplus, pension initiatives.
newsitem.headline: Clinton announces PBGC surplus, pension initiatives.

text.p: President Clinton said Monday the federal agency that insures private pensions plans had its first surplus in history last year and unveiled several measures designed to improve pension protections.

Returning to the small themes of his 1996 re-election campaign, Clinton said the measures, which include setting up a toll-free number to give workers pension information and resubmitting legislation to Congress to tighten up pension audits, aimed to help people "succeed" at home and at work.

"All the steps we announce today ... are part of our overall commitment to achieving basic retirement security for America's working families," Clinton said at the White House announcement. "Our people deserve to know that if they work hard throughout their lives, the money they worked for and that they saved is not being squandered or left unprotected."

Announcing the measures, Clinton said the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp. (PBGC), the federal agency that insures private pension plans, had turned a $869 million surplus last year, its first since the agency was created in 1974.
The agency, which as recently as 1993 had a deficit of $2.9 billion, had assets of $12.04 billion and liabilities of $11.17 billion in fiscal 1996, which ended Sept. 30.

While saying part of the improved PBGC financial position reflected robust economic growth, U.S. officials argued it was also the result of the administration's efforts to manage the agency better as well as pension reforms it passed in 1994.

Among the initiatives that Clinton announced Monday, he said he would again ask Congress to tighten the auditing of private pension plans. The legislation went to Congress last year but did not make it to a vote.

The White House said the proposal would close a loophole permitting $950 billion in pension assets to escape meaningful audits, require prompt reporting if criminal acts are found and ensure that only qualified professionals conduct audits.

The White House also announced the latest in a series of toll-free telephone hotlines, saying the Labour Department set up 1-800-998-7542 for workers to get information about their pension rights and on the warning signs of pension problems.

Clinton also drew attention to federal rules that went into effect last month requiring employers to deposit worker contributions into pension plans within 15 business days after the end of the month when the contribution was made.
The White House said it estimated that this change would increase earnings for participants and beneficiaries by a total of nearly $700 million over the next 10 years.
